proposals.relationship: Scott credits Thompson’s account of working-class protest as a formative model for making popular action politically intelligible, before her later feminist critique.
proposals.evidence_note: Scott’s 2009 retrospective, p. 35, explicitly names Thompson alongside Tilly. This bounded formative debt does not attribute her later gender analysis to Thompson or cancel her criticism. The 1988 chapter remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Scott recalls Charles Tilly’s SSRC mentorship in social theory, quantitative methods and collective action, while resisting classifications that flattened historical process.
proposals.evidence_note: Primary memoir pp. 33, 35–37, with 2024 interview corroboration. Tilly was her interdisciplinary fellowship mentor; Harvey Goldberg remained her dissertation advisor. Louise Tilly’s separate coauthorship is preserved.
primary_locators: Printed p. 33, SSRC paragraph; pp. 35–37, collective-action discussion.

proposals.relationship: Hobsbawm and Scott jointly investigate shoemakers’ radical reputation, distinguishing militant action, left allegiance and worker intellectual life instead of treating the reputation as self-explanatory.
proposals.evidence_note: Substantive opening of their joint “Political Shoemakers” read in the 1984 Worlds of Labour reprint, pp. 103–113, through a third-party transcription. Oxford verifies both authors and the original November 1980 article, pp. 86–114. Collaboration, not a one-way influence; original journal body and the rest of the reprint were not read.
primary_locators: Worlds of Labour (1984), contents and chapter heading p. 103; pp. 103–106, opening distinctions; pp. 110–113, literacy/work-organization explanations.
proposals.date_qualification: 1980 original article; 1984 reprint, not a new joint research project.
